t: Where do you work from in Bali?
s: Canggu has the density, Ubud the quiet, Sanur the people who actually want to work. All three beat a villa connection you cannot rely on.
b:
Coworking exists here for two reasons: villa internet is variable, and working alone in a villa for six months is worse than people expect.

   The areas

  Canggu   has the highest density of spaces, cafes and other remote workers, and the strongest networking. It also has the island's worst traffic and the most people who are here to talk about working.

  Ubud   is quieter, cheaper, and oriented toward wellness, creative work and longer stays. Slower pace, fewer distractions.

  Sanur   has fewer spaces and a noticeably higher proportion of people who came to work rather than to network. It suits heads down focus.

  Uluwatu and the Bukit   have a small number of spaces serving the surf community, with everything a longer drive away.

   What it costs

Day passes, weekly and monthly memberships are all standard, and monthly is far better value than daily if you are staying. Private offices and dedicated desks cost more.

Against the price of a bad video call on a failing connection, a membership is cheap insurance for anyone whose income depends on being reachable.

   Cafes versus coworking

Cafe wifi in the main areas is generally good enough for email and browsing and unreliable for calls. Bandwidth is shared, noise is unpredictable, and there is a social limit to how long one coffee holds a table.

For calls, a coworking space with call booths is the difference between sounding professional and apologising.

   The time zone problem

Bali is UTC+8. That is comfortable with Asia and Australia, workable with Europe in your afternoon, and difficult with North America.

If your team is on the US East Coast, you are looking at consistently late nights. Work out the actual meeting times before you commit to living here, because a permanent 3am schedule erodes the reason you came.

   The visa point

Working remotely from Bali requires the right permit. The E33G covers people employed by or contracted to a company established outside Indonesia.

t: What should you know about Balinese culture?
s: Ceremony is not a tourist attraction here, it is the calendar. Understanding that changes how you build, hire and live.
b:
Bali is Hindu in a country that is overwhelmingly Muslim, and religious practice is woven into daily life to a degree foreigners consistently underestimate.

   Ceremony is the calendar

Temple ceremonies, family ceremonies, cremations and village obligations are frequent and take priority. Staff will need time off for them, and it is not negotiable in the way a foreign employer might assume a day off is.

Budget for it, plan around it, and treat it as a fixed feature of operating here rather than an inconvenience. Employers who fight it lose good staff.

  Nyepi  , the day of silence in March, shuts the entire island for 24 hours including the airport. No traffic, no lights, nobody outside, guests included. Plan bookings around it.

   Banjar

The banjar is the village community organisation, and it has real authority over what happens locally: construction, ceremonies, disputes, security, waste.

If you build or operate here, your relationship with the banjar matters more than most foreign owners expect. It can affect construction access, noise complaints, staff and whether small problems get resolved quietly or escalate.

Introduce yourself. Contribute when asked. This is not corruption, it is community obligation, and it is how the system works.

   Practical etiquette

  Step over offerings on the pavement, not on them
  Cover shoulders and knees at temples; a sarong is usually provided or required
  Do not enter a temple during menstruation, which is a stated rule rather than a suggestion
  Use the right hand for giving and receiving
  Do not touch heads, including children's
  Feet are impolite; do not point them at people or shrines
  Public anger loses you standing; raised voices are read as loss of control, not authority

That last one matters commercially. Negotiating hard is fine. Shouting marks you as someone to be managed rather than dealt with.

t: How bad are Bali's water and waste problems?
s: Groundwater depletion and waste management are the island's real constraints, and both are becoming regulatory risks for property owners.
b:
This is the part of Bali that the marketing does not cover, and it increasingly affects owners commercially rather than only ethically.

   Water

Bali's water demand has grown far faster than its supply. Tourism is water intensive: pools, laundry, showers, golf, landscaping. Groundwater extraction has increased accordingly, and in parts of the south the water table has fallen.

For a property owner this shows up three ways:

  Operating cost.   Where piped supply is absent or insufficient, trucked water is a real recurring expense that rises in dry season.

  Regulatory risk.   Groundwater extraction is regulated and scrutiny has been increasing. A villa whose entire supply depends on an unpermitted well is carrying a risk that has been getting larger, not smaller.

  Long term viability.   A development model built on unlimited cheap groundwater is not a safe assumption for a twenty five year lease.

The Bukit is the sharpest example: limestone geology, little accessible groundwater, and many properties reliant on trucked supply.

   Waste

Bali's waste infrastructure has not kept pace with either population or tourism. Collection is inconsistent outside the main areas, landfill capacity is strained, and a significant share of waste is burned or ends up in rivers.

In wet season the rivers carry it to the beaches, which is why images of rubbish on Kuta beach circulate every year. It is seasonal, it is real, and it affects the product you are selling to guests.

   What owners can actually do

  Arrange proper waste collection rather than assuming it happens
  Separate and use the private recycling operations that exist
  Avoid burning, which is common and genuinely harmful
  Install water efficient fittings and a pool cover, which cuts evaporation substantially
  Harvest rainwater, which is straightforward here given the wet season volume
  Ensure any well is properly permitted
  Treat wastewater properly rather than to the minimum
